summary: This Wikipedia-derived note describes the State of the Union address, the speech a U.S. President gives to a joint session of Congress under Article II, Section 3 of the Constitution. It explains the address's purpose of reporting on the nation's condition and outlining the President's legislative agenda and priorities. The note also traces its history, from George Washington's first annual message in 1790 through Thomas Jefferson's 1801 shift to written reports and Woodrow Wilson's 1913 revival of in-person delivery.
one_line: Overview of the U.S. President's State of the Union address to Congress, its constitutional basis, and its history from 1790 onward.
key_facts: The State of the Union address fulfills rules in Article II, Section 3 of the U.S. Constitution, which requires the President to periodically give Congress information on the state of the union and recommend necessary and expedient measures.
The address is a speech by the President of the United States to a joint session of the United States Congress, except in the first year of a new president's term.
During most of the country's first century, the President primarily only submitted a written report to Congress.
Woodrow Wilson, the 28th U.S. President, began the regular practice of delivering the address to Congress in person after 1913 as a way to rally support for his agenda.
George Washington delivered the first regular annual message before a joint session of Congress on January 8, 1790, in New York City, then the provisional U.S. capital.
In 1801, Thomas Jefferson discontinued the practice of delivering the address in person, regarding it as too monarchical, similar to the Speech from the Throne.
Under Jefferson's practice, the address was written and sent to Congress to be read by a clerk until 1913, when Woodrow Wilson re-established in-person delivery despite some initial controversy.
Presidents during the latter half of the 20th century sent written State of the Union addresses rather than delivering them in person.
Jimmy Carter was the last President to send a written State of the Union address, in 1981, after his defeat by Ronald Reagan and days before his term ended.
With the advent of radio and television, the address is now broadcast live across the country on many networks.
